sysd-reliab-015.title: Authentication: proving who you are
sysd-reliab-015.text:
A password does not prove who you are. Like a key card, it implies authenticity without guaranteeing it. Authentication is the act of proving an assertion, such as the identity of a computer system user.

Two ideas are easy to blur. Identification only indicates who a person or thing is, while authentication is the process of verifying that claim. In computing, a user's identity often has to be verified before confidential data or systems can be reached.

Authentication is also distinct from permission checking, which {{ref:sysd-reliab-030}} covers. Authentication verifies that you are who you say you are. Permission checking verifies that you are allowed to do what you are trying to do. It often follows authentication but does not presuppose it, because an anonymous agent could be authorized for a limited set of actions.

Trust has to come from somewhere. Most secure internet communication relies on centralized trust. In HTTPS, public certificate authorities vouch for the authenticity of websites, and {{ref:sysd-reliab-024}} rests on the same model, with companies such as Google authenticating users for other applications. The alternative is decentralized, peer-based trust. In a web of trust, as in PGP, individuals personally verify and sign each other's cryptographic keys, with no central authority.

sysd-reliab-127.title: Cross-site scripting: when a page runs an attacker's code
sysd-reliab-127.text:
A browser trusts a page because of where it came from, and cross-site scripting exploits exactly that. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a web-application vulnerability that lets attackers inject client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users. Under the same-origin policy, content from URLs with the same scheme, host name and port gets the same permissions, as {{ref:sysd-found-074}} explains. The injected script arrives from the trusted site, so it runs with that site's permissions and can reach session cookies.

The kinds differ in where the script hides. In reflected XSS, a server uses client data, usually query parameters, to build a page without sanitizing it, as when a search page echoes the query. Stored XSS is more devastating: the server saves the attacker's data and shows it to other users, as on a message board that lets users post HTML. In DOM-based XSS the data never touches the server, because the page's own JavaScript reflects it into the page. It is a case of code injection, grouped under Injection in the 2021 and 2025 editions of the OWASP Top 10.

sysd-reliab-016.title: Authentication factors: know, have, are
sysd-reliab-016.text:
Every way of proving who you are draws on one of three kinds of evidence. Authentication factors are the three categories of evidence used to verify identity: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is. Each factor covers a range of elements used to verify a person's identity before granting access, approving a transaction, or signing a document.

Knowledge factors are things the user knows, such as a password, passphrase, PIN, challenge-response or security question. Ownership factors are things the user has: an ID card, a security token, or a cell phone holding a software token. Inherence factors are what the user is or does, such as a fingerprint, retinal pattern, face, voice, signature or other biometric identifier.

Security research has determined that a positive authentication should verify elements from at least two factors, and preferably all three. Even the strongest-sounding factor can disappoint. Fingerprints were historically the most authoritative method, but court cases in the US and elsewhere have raised fundamental doubts about their reliability.

sysd-reliab-120.title: Salt: why identical passwords should not look identical
sysd-reliab-120.text:
Two users pick the same password, and anyone reading an unsalted password database can see it, because identical passwords give identical hashes. A salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes a password or passphrase, as {{ref:sysd-reliab-106}} explains. The system concatenates salt and password, hashes the result, and stores the hash with the salt. The salt needs no encryption, since knowing it would not help the attacker.

A fresh salt for each password gives different hashes for the same password. It also forces an attacker to hash each guess separately against every entry. And it defeats the precomputed tables described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-121}}, since building a table for every unique salt is not viable. A salt of 16 bytes (128 bits) or more is generally sufficient. Reusing one salt is dangerous: a table that accounts for it becomes viable, and cracking one hash exposes others with the same password.

sysd-reliab-030.title: Authorization: deciding what you may do
sysd-reliab-030.text:
Knowing who someone is settles nothing until the system decides what that person may do. Authorization is the function of specifying rights to access resources, usually through an access policy, and then deciding whether a particular subject may access a particular resource. Subjects can be human users, software or hardware. Resources can be files, data, programs, devices or application functions.

Access control enforces the policy by approving or rejecting access requests from authenticated consumers. Identity and access management runs in two phases. A configuration phase creates the user account and defines its access policy. In the usage phase, authentication comes first and access control follows. Consumers should get only what they need to do their jobs, an idea covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-126}}.

Maintaining this data is not trivial. It often costs as much administration as managing credentials, because changing a user's authorization means changing or deleting the matching access rules. Broken authorization is often listed as the number one risk in web applications.

sysd-reliab-022.title: OAuth 2.0: access without sharing your password
sysd-reliab-022.text:
You can give an application a narrow view of your account without ever handing over your password. That is the promise of OAuth 2.0. It is an open standard for access delegation that lets a user grant an application consented access to resources on another site without sharing credentials. An app holding an OAuth token can reach only the parts of the user's profile that the user allowed.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol. It is designed primarily to grant access to a set of resources such as remote APIs or a user's data. Four roles take part. The resource owner owns the protected resources, and the client needs access to them. The authorization server issues tokens, described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-134}}, after authentication and consent. The resource server validates the tokens and returns resources. Scopes specify exactly why access may be granted, and the acceptable scope values depend on the resource server.

OAuth 1 is specified in RFC 5849 and OAuth 2 in RFC 6749. The newer version has critics. Singh lists three common disadvantages: it lacks built-in security features, has no standard implementation, and has no common set of scopes. Eran Hammer, a former lead author, argued that OAuth 2.0 became more complex, less interoperable and less secure than 1.0. He blamed the removal of protocol-level signatures and cryptography, and the many items left for implementations to decide.

sysd-reliab-126.title: Least privilege: only what the job needs
sysd-reliab-126.text:
An account that only creates backups may run backup applications, and it cannot install software. That is the principle of least privilege in miniature. Every module, such as a process, user or program, should be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

The payoff comes in three ways. Limiting what code can do system-wide means a vulnerability in one application cannot be used to exploit the rest of the machine. Code with limited scope is easier to test for its possible actions and interactions. And the fewer privileges an application requires, the easier it is to deploy.

Jerome Saltzer's original formulation says every program and every privileged user should operate with the least amount of privilege necessary to complete the job. The idea is associated with privilege bracketing: assume privileges at the last possible moment and dismiss them as soon as they are unnecessary. True least privilege is hard, though. Practice removes the privileges judged unnecessary, which leaves more than the true minimum.

sysd-reliab-017.title: Multi-factor authentication: more than one proof
sysd-reliab-017.text:
A stolen password opens every account that asks for nothing else. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) closes that gap. It grants a user access only after they present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to an authentication mechanism. The premise is that an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply every factor. If one is missing or wrong, access stays blocked. Accounts with MFA enabled are significantly less likely to be compromised.

Two-factor authentication is the special case of exactly two factors, such as a bank card together with a PIN. Stacking checks of one kind adds nothing: a fingerprint, a face and a PIN with a day code is still two-factor. Single-factor authentication, the weakest level, offers little protection from misuse. 

Rules have caught up with the practice. PCI DSS requirement 8.3 requires MFA for remote access into a card data environment. The second Payment Services Directive has required strong customer authentication on most electronic payments in the European Economic Area since 14 September 2019.

sysd-reliab-034.title: Why OAuth is not a login system
sysd-reliab-034.text:
A valet key gives access without saying who is holding it, and an OAuth token works the same way. That is why using OAuth on its own as a login method, called pseudo-authentication, is a trap. OAuth says nothing about who the user is.

The client asked for a token, got one and used it, without knowing who authorized it or whether a user was there at all. Much of the point of OAuth is delegated access where the user is not present. That is bad for authentication, where the point is to find out who is there.

The temptation is understandable, because the issuing service usually authenticates the user along the way. OAuth was not designed for login, though, and the assumption can cause major security flaws. A stolen valet key lets an attacker impersonate its user to any application relying on OAuth2 for pseudo-authentication against the same authorization server. The approach in {{ref:sysd-reliab-036}} avoids this, because its response is an assertion of identity and cryptographic verification prevents the theft. The fix built on OAuth itself is {{ref:sysd-reliab-024}}.

sysd-reliab-018.title: Continuous authentication: checking all session long
sysd-reliab-018.text: Most computer systems check who you are once, at log-in, and trust you from then on. That can be a critical security flaw. Continuous authentication keeps monitoring and verifying a user throughout a session, based on biometric traits, instead of only at the initial log-in. Smartphone sensors can extract behavioral attributes such as touch dynamics, keystroke dynamics and gait recognition, which verify users implicitly and continuously. Systems built on these behavioral traits are known as active or continuous authentication systems.

sysd-reliab-019.title: Digital authentication: proving identity over a network
sysd-reliab-019.text: Digital authentication, also called electronic authentication, is a group of processes that establish and present confidence in user identities to an information system by electronic methods. It is technically challenging, because users are authenticated remotely over a network. In NIST's generic model, an applicant proves their identity to a credential service provider (CSP) and becomes a subscriber. The subscriber receives an authenticator, such as a token, plus credentials such as a user name. The subscriber then proves possession of the authenticator to a relying party, the service being used, in a session. A man-in-the-middle can pose as both parties, so extra identity factors may be required.

sysd-reliab-031.title: Access control models: how a policy is written
sysd-reliab-031.text:
A rule about who may do what has to be written down somehow, and the way it is written decides how it is checked. Access control models are the ways an authorization policy is expressed and checked, such as lists, roles, attributes and relationships.

Authorizations are expressed as access policies, for example as a capability or as the kind of list described in {{ref:sysd-q-010}}. In the role-based model, subjects get one or more roles, and access is allowed when the resource has been assigned at least one of them {{ref:sysd-q-014}} covers it. A model based on relationships is gaining prominence with the rise of social media, and {{ref:sysd-q-083}} covers that one.

A policy language can go further. One framework is policy-based and attribute-based, so it can weigh attributes of the user, action, resource and context. It supplies the policy language that OAuth lacks, while OAuth handles consent and access delegation. That framework is {{ref:sysd-q-082}}.

sysd-reliab-028.title: A security checklist for system design
sysd-reliab-028.text:
Security is easier to build in than to bolt on, so one guide lists what a design should cover by default. Secure design protects sensitive information and keeps the infrastructure stable. The guide's key design points are authentication, authorization, encryption, vulnerability, network security, terminal security, container security, API security, audit and compliance, emergency responses, third-party vendors and disaster recovery.

A few points show how the pieces fit. Multiple factors work because an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply them all. The standard in {{ref:sysd-reliab-124}} verifies identity with digital signatures rather than shared passwords. Passwords are stored as salted hashes, with a unique salt per password. Authorization follows least privilege.

Under vulnerability, XSS lets attackers inject scripts into pages other users view, and contextual output encoding counters it. Forged requests, the subject of {{ref:sysd-reliab-129}}, are countered by embedding extra authentication data, such as unique tokens, in requests. Zero trust does not trust users and devices by default, even on a corporate LAN. In transit, OAuth forbids sending tokens or passwords in the clear and requires TLS on its endpoints.

sysd-reliab-021.title: Sessions, tokens and other ways to stay logged in
sysd-reliab-021.text:
After you log in once, a website has to recognize you on every later request, and it has six common ways to manage a logged-in user's identity.

With a session, the server stores the user's identity and gives the browser a session ID cookie, which lets the server track login state. Cookies do not work well across devices. With a token, the identity is encoded into a token that the browser sends on later requests. The server needs no session storage, though tokens need encryption and decryption. A standard format for such tokens uses digital signatures for trust; {{ref:sysd-reliab-032}} explains it. The signature travels inside the token, so no server session is needed.

The other three methods involve a second party or device. A central authentication service can make one login work across multiple sites, which {{ref:sysd-reliab-025}} covers. OAuth 2.0 lets one site get limited access to your data on another site without being given your passwords. QR-code login encodes a random token into a QR code, and scanning it logs the user in on mobile without typing a password.

sysd-reliab-129.title: Cross-site request forgery: abusing a site's trust in your browser
sysd-reliab-129.text:
Your browser will vouch for you to any site that holds your cookie, even when you did not ask it to. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an exploit in which a web application receives unauthorized commands from a user that it trusts. An innocent user is tricked into submitting a request they did not intend, through image tags, hidden forms or JavaScript, which changes session state or the user's account.

It works because browsers automatically and invisibly include a domain's cookies in any request to that domain. A forged request from another page therefore looks genuine. Unlike XSS, which exploits the trust a user has in a site, CSRF exploits the trust a site has in a user's browser.

An attack needs a site without CSRF protection, a state-changing action, input values the attacker can determine, and a victim who is logged in. GET is meant to be safe, yet a GET can be forged with an IMG tag. Applications that use GET to change state should switch to POST or add anti-CSRF protection.

sysd-reliab-134.title: The access token: a key with limits
sysd-reliab-134.text:
Every request in an OAuth exchange rides on one small string. An access token is a credential, usually an opaque string, representing an authorization issued to the client for accessing protected resources. It represents specific scopes and durations of access, granted by the resource owner and enforced by the resource server and authorization server. A token may be an identifier used to look up the authorization information, or it may carry that information itself, as data plus a signature.

The token replaces a username and password with a single credential the resource server understands. It can be more restrictive than the grant that produced it, which spares the resource server many authentication methods. The client should request the minimal scope necessary. The server may issue less, and it must say what scope it granted.

The client presents the token to the resource server to reach protected resources. Tokens must not be forgeable or guessable, so the chance of guessing one should stay at or below 2^(-128). They must stay confidential and travel only over TLS.

sysd-reliab-135.title: Refresh tokens: short-lived access that renews
sysd-reliab-135.text:
An access token should expire quickly, and the refresh token is what makes that bearable. A refresh token is a credential the authorization server issues to the client for obtaining new access tokens. When the current token expires or becomes invalid, the client uses it to get a new one. That lets access tokens be short-lived and carry fewer permissions than the owner authorized.

Issuing a refresh token is optional. Unlike access tokens, refresh tokens are intended only for authorization servers and are never sent to resource servers. When the access token expires, the client authenticates with the authorization server and presents the refresh token. The server validates it and issues a new access token and, optionally, a new refresh token. The requested scope must not exceed the original grant, and the token is bound to the client it was issued to.

Rotation reveals theft. The server issues a new refresh token with each refresh and invalidates the old one, so the attacker or the legitimate client will eventually present an invalidated token. Refresh tokens must be kept confidential.

sysd-reliab-032.title: JSON Web Tokens: identity that carries its own proof
sysd-reliab-032.text:
A JSON Web Token carries its own proof inside it. A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an Internet standard for creating data, optionally signed and optionally encrypted, whose JSON payload asserts a number of claims. It is a Proposed Standard, RFC 7519, and relies on the JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption standards.

A JWT has three parts: a header naming the signing algorithm, a payload containing a set of claims, and a signature that validates the token. Each part is Base64url-encoded and the parts are joined with periods. The signature is computed over the encoded header and payload, typically with HMAC using SHA-256 (HS256) or an RSA signature with SHA-256 (RS256). One party, usually the server, signs with its private key. Anyone holding the matching public key can verify the token.

Tokens are compact and URL-safe. The client sends the JWT in the Authorization header with the Bearer schema. User state is never kept in server memory and the token is self-contained, so this is stateless and avoids repeated database queries.

sysd-reliab-024.title: OpenID Connect: login built on OAuth
sysd-reliab-024.text:
OAuth 2.0 can tell an application what it may reach, but not who is knocking. OpenID Connect fills that gap. It is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds login and profile information about the person who is logged in. Clients can verify an end user's identity from the authorization server's authentication and fetch basic profile information.

It specifies a RESTful HTTP API with JSON as the data format, so web, mobile and JavaScript clients can ask about authenticated sessions and end users. The current application is the relying party. The provider gives it a one-time code, which the token endpoint exchanges for an access code valid for an hour. The token arrives in the format of {{ref:sysd-reliab-032}}. The relying party then calls the UserInfo endpoint with a secure token to learn about the end user.

Because it sits on top of OAuth, it has a built-in permission layer that asks the user to agree to what the service provider may access. The older standard in {{ref:sysd-reliab-027}} achieves consent only by developer hard-coding.

sysd-reliab-138.title: JWT claims: the statements inside a token
sysd-reliab-138.text:
A token is only as useful as what it says. The claims of a JWT are the name/value members of the JSON object, called the JWT Claims Set, that the token conveys. Claim names fall into three classes: registered, public and private. Private names are agreed between producer and consumer and can collide, so they need caution. The registered claims are a starting point, not a mandatory set, and each application defines which it uses.

The common ones tell a service who issued the token and for whom. The iss claim names the issuer, sub names the subject, and iat records when the token was issued. The aud claim lists the intended recipients. If it is present and the processor is not named, the JWT must be rejected. A token must not be accepted on or after its exp time, nor before its nbf time. Implementers may allow a few minutes of leeway for clock skew. The jti claim gives the token a unique identifier, which can prevent replay.

sysd-reliab-139.title: Creating and validating a JWT, step by step
sysd-reliab-139.text:
Making a JWT is a short recipe, and checking one is the same recipe run backward, with a rejection at every step. Creating a JWT builds a claims set and then signs or encrypts it. Validating one reverses those steps and rejects the token if any step fails.

To create one, build the Claims Set, take its UTF-8 octets (bytes) as the message, and build a JOSE header. Then sign the message as a JWS payload (a JSON Web Signature) or encrypt it as JWE plaintext (a JSON Web Encryption). No canonicalization is needed. For nested signing or encryption, the resulting JWS or JWE becomes the new message and the steps repeat with a cty header value of JWT. Otherwise that JWS or JWE is the finished JWT.

Validation starts by checking that the JWT contains at least one period. The part before the first period is base64url-decoded into a JOSE header, which must be valid JSON and contain only parameters the implementation understands and supports. The validator then decides whether the JWT is a JWS or a JWE, and validates the signature or decrypts accordingly. If the header's cty value is JWT, the message is itself a nested JWT and validation starts again on it. Otherwise the message is base64url-decoded and must be valid JSON, which becomes the Claims Set.

If any step fails, the JWT must be rejected as invalid input. Even a JWT that validates should be rejected unless its algorithms are acceptable, because which algorithms may be used is an application decision.

sysd-reliab-130.title: Stopping CSRF: tokens, cookies and headers
sysd-reliab-130.text:
A forged request can carry the victim's cookies, but it cannot carry a secret the attacker never sees. Most CSRF defenses build on that. They embed extra authentication data in requests so the application can spot requests from unauthorized locations.

The synchronizer token pattern embeds a secret, unique token in every HTML form and verifies it on the server. The attacker cannot put a correct token in forged requests. In the cookie-to-header technique, the server sets a random token cookie, and JavaScript copies it into a custom HTTP header. The server validates the token. A double submit cookie sets the token as a cookie and as a hidden form field, then checks that they match. The server stores no token, but a site with cookie-setting functionality can bypass the scheme.

Two defenses lean on the browser. The SameSite cookie attribute set to strict makes the browser send the cookie only on same-site requests, which defeats CSRF if the browser implements it correctly. Checking the Origin or Referer header is another approach, and a request omitting Referer must count as unauthorized.
